title: 2028 Volvo XC60: Prices, Reviews & Pictures - CarGurus.com
summary: Explore the 2028 Volvo XC60 with CarGurus reviews, pricing insights, comparisons, news and expert analysis.
body_markdown:
## Look & feel


8/10


Even with a refresh in 2026, the XC60 gets a few significant design changes for 2028, including restyled front and rear bumpers, updated Thor’s Hammer (that refers to the shape) Matrix LED headlights, and revised interior styling with open-pore wood trim and dash accents. This model year also introduces the new Heather Bronze color that changes from a light brown to a rose gold depending on the light.


Even with the styling changes, the XC60 doesn’t look drastically different on the outside, and it is essentially a pared-down version of the XC90. The interior is a study in minimalism with a clean dash, a large 11.2-inch screen, and few buttons and dials to mar the clean aesthetic. Some will dislike the large vertical screen as it looks like an iPad tacked on the dash as an afterthought, but we thought it was fairly well integrated, with the air vents flanking the screen like wings. And while most of the climate controls are operated through the screen, attractively styled manual knobs still control the direction of the airflow.


We drove the top-tier Ultra trim level with a new light brown interior and tailored dash. The light wood and textiles on the dash blend well with the slightly darker Cardamom leather seats. From the stitching to the piping to the etched Swedish flag below the outboard air vents, the overall effect is both simple and elegant. The materials throughout the cabin are well done, and the fit and finish is solid.


## Performance


6/10


All-wheel drive remains standard on all trims, and the 2028 Volvo XC60 carries over the base 247-horsepower, 2.0-liter turbocharged four-cylinder engine in the B5 AWD model. The T8 AWD PHEV, however, receives a massive update with a significantly larger battery, more power, and 43 miles of extra electric range. Both the B5 and T8 come with an eight-speed automatic transmission. The T8 shares the same core engine as the B5, but the 41.2-kWh battery and larger rear motor mean the T8 delivers 455 hp and 560 pound-feet of torque and 78 miles of all-electric range. The total gas and electric range maxes out at 590 miles.


During our two-day test in Copenhagen, Denmark, we only had access to the T8 models in the top-tier Ultra trim. While this model delivers a generally smooth ride and has decent power, the acceleration feels more sluggish than the numbers promise. We toggled through the various drive modes from Hybrid to Power to Pure and experienced the same lag when accelerating from a stop in each mode. Even when we were in Pure mode, where instantaneous torque should have been available, there was noticeable lag. Highway passing maneuvers were fine, but still not quite the belly-flipping acceleration we’d expect from a turbocharged engine with 455 hp.


We were driving European-spec models, and were able to test the various speed-limit notifications on the XC60. Drivers can toggle this on or off in the infotainment screen and set it to an audible or a speed-dampening alert. We tried out both options and found the beep annoying, but the speed dampener was quite helpful. The power decreases as drivers approach a speed limit, which lets them know they're reaching it. Of course, it's possible to push through it, but the dampening is super helpful to keep the car within the speed limit, and we really wish this were a feature common on U.S. vehicles. In a place filled with speed cameras, such as Chicago, we could see where this would be a useful tool.


Refinement was decent in the XC60, especially in Pure mode or while cruising at highway speeds in gas, electric, or hybrid modes, as very little road or tire noise creeps into the cabin. However, when the engine was engaged, we could hear it a little more than we wanted to.


## Form & function


7/10


Assuming buyers don’t need a third row, the XC60 is a great small-to-midsize, five-passenger luxury SUV with competitive rear legroom and a lot of clever storage spaces, including netted pockets on the back of the front seats. Rear cargo volume, however, is at the bottom of the pack in terms of the competitive set, with just 21.6 cubic feet behind the second row and a maximum cargo capacity of 54.5 cubic feet.


One feature we found particularly helpful on the Ultra trim was the Active Air Suspension, which allows drivers to raise and lower the suspension via power buttons in the cargo area. This is not only helpful for loading but also for dogs jumping into the back. It’s standard on the Ultra and available on the Plus trim level. Also at the rear, the power liftgate is height-adjustable, which is great for shorter drivers and garages with low ceilings.


Available features include heated rear seats, quad-zone climate controls, a 12-volt power outlet in the cargo area, and front and rear USB-C charge ports. For skiers or those who habitually carry long, narrow items, there’s a ski pass-through in the center of the rear seat in addition to 40/60 split-folding seats.


## Technology


8/10


The XC60 is equipped with Google built-in as well as Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. The big tech upgrade for 2028, though, is the addition of Gemini AI, which replaces the Google Assistant. We’ve recently started playing around with ChatGPT via Apple CarPlay in test vehicles and found it helpful to tell us practical information about towns we’re driving through or buildings we’re passing. Gemini does this and more as it can also access vehicle systems such as temperature controls with natural voice commands, and if there’s something drivers can’t figure out how to adjust in the car because it’s buried in a screen, Gemini will access the owner’s manual and point out where it’s located if it can’t make the change itself. The caveat is that Google AI features come with a four-year trial, after which they require a subscription.


The 11.2-inch screen was new for 2026, and even though the user interface gets a slight update for 2028, drivers still have to tap-tap through the menu settings in the screen for most vehicle settings. Drive mode settings are through the screen. Audio controls, except the volume knob, are through the screen. And so on. While a lot of this is something an owner would get used to and eventually navigate proficiently, during our short time with the vehicles, we found ourselves relying on Gemini a lot to figure out where the various vehicle settings were, lest we were reprimanded by the driver-attention monitor for looking at the screen too much.


Thankfully, unlike the electric vehicles from Volvo, mirror and steering-wheel settings are still physical controls.


The Ultra trim level we tested had all the tech goodies buyers could possibly want, including highly adjustable front seats, memory seat settings for the driver and front passenger, and a 3D surround-view camera with high resolution. While the XC60 does come with a wireless phone charger, it’s not one of the good ones. It's OK for short periods, but anything longer than 30 minutes on the charger turns a phone into a hand warmer.


## Safety


8/10


As we'd expect from a Volvo, there’s a lot of standard safety equipment. All XC60s get automatic emergency braking, a cyclist door opening alert, blind-spot monitors, adaptive cruise control, automatic reverse braking, rear cross-traffic alert, lane-keep assist, front and rear parking sensors, and road-sign recognition. New features for 2028 include available automatic emergency steering, lane-change assist, Matrix LED headlights, and the 3D surround-view camera.


Even though our test was brief, we had a couple of encounters with the safety systems. The first was right out of the gate in city traffic, when we'd already started braking as traffic slowed. Apparently, we weren’t slowing down fast enough, and the safety systems intervened by slamming on the brakes hard and then sucking us swiftly back into the seats with the seat belts. The second instance was when we were turning into our hotel parking lot, and the vehicle jumped at a shadow or perceived obstacle, again slamming on the brakes to ensure we didn’t hit anything. It was all a bit aggressive, but better safe than sorry, we suppose.


The adaptive cruise control worked well enough and didn’t feel jerky as it slowed with highway traffic. While it will never replace human eyes, it’s definitely a useful tool on a long, bland highway drive. The other feature we truly appreciated was the surround-view camera that reports proximity to an obstacle—and it’s actually accurate. We were traveling with a tape measure and got out to verify the distance when we were backing into a parking space. It was spot on.


At the time of writing neither the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) nor the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) had crash tested the 2028 XC60. However, the IIHS gave the 2027 model a mix of Good and Acceptable crashworthiness and crash-avoidance scores, while the NHTSA gave it a five-star overall safety rating.


## Cost-effectiveness


7/10


The 2028 Volvo XC60 is due out in the first quarter of 2027, and at the time of writing, pricing for that model year was not yet available. However, we can make some general assumptions based on the 2027 model year pricing. The B5 model is competitively priced with three trims: Core, Plus, and Ultra. It falls in the middle of the pack, less expensive than the BMW X3 and the Audi Q5 but more expensive than the Lexus NX and the Mercedes-Benz GLC. However, the price span for the base trims of these models is about $3,000, and they all start at around $50,000.


Switching to the T8 model and comparing it against the Mercedes and the Lexus PHEVs, the price disparity is significant because the XC60 drops the base Core trim for that lineup. However, if buyers are going to plug in their PHEV religiously at home, the higher price tag could be worthwhile in the long run because the Volvo's all-electric range bests the Mercedes and Lexus ranges by 24 miles and 33 miles, respectively.


While we appreciated the premium amenities on our Ultra test vehicle, we didn’t necessarily need all of them. For those who like the Volvo look and don’t want the PHEV powertrain, the Core model is well equipped with a lot of premium amenities, including Gemini and a ton of safety features. For our money, we’d level up to the Plus trim, which adds the likes of the Harman Kardon premium audio system and the surround-view camera. That would keep the price point at less than $60,000 if buyers opt for the B5. For those who really and truly will charge their vehicle (seriously) and do a lot of city driving, we’d recommend the T8 because it's possible to stay in Pure electric mode most of the time, saving trips to the gas station. And drivers still have that extra range when they need it.
